<reason>Both sides were sharp, disciplined, and stayed on the motion, and both handled the Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure correctly. B (PRO) built the cleaner decision rule — "when 'Buy' turns out to be a lie, who eats the loss?" — and defended it through the whole exchange. B neutralized A's two strongest openings: the replication scare was answered by a clear, consistently applied rule (one license, one successor account, per generation; five children, one library), and the privacy attack was blunted by pointing out that the platform already holds the ashamed reader's history, that paper shelves and diaries already pass by default, and that wills/settings already solve exclusion. B's most durable line, "a guarantee is a floor; a label is a menu the seller writes," directly exposed the structural weakness of A's alternative: A's remedy depends on platforms voluntarily offering the inheritable product, and A itself conceded the subscription-flight logic that platforms would rather not offer it. B's pressure question about the family of someone who already spent thousands drew A's weakest answer — restitution/refunds/damages — which B then crystallized devastatingly as a widow litigating a Kindle library title by title. A's best work came late and was genuinely good: the sublicensing/upstream-rights mechanism and the closing reframe that a statutory access right is only a claim against a fragile corporate promise, whereas a portable file is something you can hold. That is a real live route, but it partly proves too much (it also undercuts A's own lifetime non-revocation mandate), it arrives mostly in Rebuttal 2 and closing, and A never explains why mandating DRM-free portability is an easier ask upstream than mandating one supervised transfer. B also landed the jujitsu that A's "modest" fix is the larger grant. A's late claim that the guarantee could only bind future sales was asserted without support in the final speech. Net: B made the decisive clash easier to resolve.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's answer to the waivability trap — "a guarantee is a floor; a label is a menu the seller writes," plus the observation that A had described designation as a product platforms *may* sell — converted A's cleverest pressure question into a demonstration that A's remedy leaves the outcome to the very party that wrote the misleading word. Paired with B's closing skewering of A's restitution answer as "the windfall, wearing a suit," this was the decisive exchange.</best_rebuttal>
